newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - Sarajevo skiers hope to restore Olympic glories.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Sarajevo skiers hope to restore Olympic glories.

text.p: Skis will soon be swishing over the debris of war on the bleak mountains outside Sarajevo, with alpine enthusiasts hoping to bring back the Olympic spirit to ethnically riven Bosnia.

In a landscape of torched hotels, pines split by artillery fire and mine fields, the company that ran Sarajevo's 1984 Winter Olympic games has begun to rebuild the shattered sports facilities that welcomed world athletes 12 years ago.

A metre (three feet) of fresh snow, the arrival of lift equipment from Austria and dogged determination should see the start of the first post-war skiing on the Bjelasnica and Igman mountains, southwest of the Bosnian capital, this month.
"We hope to bring back something of the quality of life that Sarajevans enjoyed before the war," said Enes Terzic, general manager of the Sarajevo Olympic Centre.
It will be a slow start to a long job. In the summer of 1993 a Bosnian Serb army offensive captured the Igman and Bjelasnica mountains amid heavy fighting.
Fearing the Serb bid to tighten the siege of Sarajevo would cause a humanitarian catastrophe, world leaders put pressure on the army of General Ratko Mladic to withdraw.

As the soldiers left they firebombed the mountain hotels, tore down power lines and took away ski equipment in a scorched earth policy that left little standing. The Sarajevo ski company inherited a wasteland.
LOANS AND DONATIONS HELPED REBUILDING
A $900,000 U.S. charity project to restore electricity to nearby villages also brought back power to the ski area. A $300,000 loan enabled the Olympic Centre to buy a ski tow.
Donations of safety and technical equipment from Swedish, Italian and Austrian companies will open up around 30 percent of the old ski area.

Terzic predicts a frantic rush of Sarajevo ski fanatics blocking the worn-out roads up the mountain. He scoffed at reports they would be put off by mines and unexploded ordnance, which he assured had been carefully cleared away.

"I'm ready to claim tens of thousands of Sarajevans will come to ski," he said. They will pay 10 German marks ($6) a day, a pittance compared to European costs but a substantial sum in Bosnia's war-worn economy.

On the mountain groups of workers were toiling through waist-deep snow with shovels to dig free machinery. Much of the first wave of renovations has been of small tows for children to use on nursery slopes.
"I think these baby lifts are the most important," said Fehim Mirojevic, the Bjelasnica sports director, "I've lost a generation of young skiers so I need to start again."
Mirojevic said only 3,000 people a day, compared to at least 10,000 before the war, would fit on the mountain.
A gala opening competition is planned for January. Italian ski star and Olympic gold medallist Alberto Tomba, a driving force behind the project, is due to be there.

"We are forming an international fund for the rebuilding of all the sports facilities here," said Terzic. "One of its godfathers is Tomba and we've had lots of help from other Olympic cities and from resorts like Sestriere in Italy."
LONG TERM PLANS

Within three years Terzic said he hoped to have rebuilt all the existing facilities, including the luxury hotels now just blackened shells, and to have begun an ambitious expansion programme across the peaks and valleys of the Igman range.
The plans ignore the biggest problem facing Sarajevo skiers -- their favourite pistes are on another mountain, to the southeast of the city, which is firmly in Bosnian Serb hands.

Bjelasnica is cold and exposed, but the Jahorina complex is sheltered by high trees, its hotels are intact and its lift equipment has run every winter throughout the war. But no Moslem would dare to travel there.

The ethnic barriers which show no sign of coming down bring few benefits to Serb skiers. Some of the hotels are occupied by refugees, others by government officials. There is no money for renovations and little hope of attracting investment.

"Without Sarajevo we can never expect to get the thousands of people who used to come here," said Dragan Sokolovic, deputy manager of the Jahorina Olympic Centre. "We will exist, we can survive, but it will not be the same."
Terzic, whose company claims it owns the Jahorina complex, says he is determined to recover his property.

"Yes, but how?" responded Sokolovic. "Now it's on the Serb side." A few hundred people are expected to ski every day on Jahorina, where indicted war criminal Mladic appeared on the slopes last year, to the delight of television cameramen.

"For the opening contest we'll invite skiers from the Republika Srpska (Bosnian Serb republic)," said Terzic. "We are approaching this with the Olympic spirit, without any political prejudice. We want Sarajevo to be a true Olympic city again."
Many Sarajevans wish the spirit would embrace both mountains.

"Jahorina was where the city went to ski. It is very depressing we still can't go there," said Damir, 25. "Really, I'd swap that cold and draughty Bjelasnica for just a tiny piece of Jahorina if they'd give it to us."
